opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a question I get a lot, and I think the honest answer is that it's more nuanced than people expect. There's a common narrative that biology is data-poor and that's what holds everything back. In some ways that's true, but I think it can be the wrong framing.

If you look at something like protein structure prediction, the Protein Data Bank isn't enormous by modern machine learning standards. We're talking about a couple hundred thousand structures, not billions of tokens of internet text. Yet with the right architecture, the right inductive biases, and clever use of things like evolutionary information from sequence databases, you could get models that generalize remarkably well. So the lesson I take from that is that it's not just about raw quantity. It's about how much signal you can extract from what you have, and how well your model is set up to capture the underlying physics and chemistry.

Where data really does become a bottleneck is when you move closer to the questions we care about in drug design. Things like binding affinity, selectivity, toxicity, how a molecule behaves in a cell or in a patient. That data is much sparser, noisier, often generated in different labs under different conditions, and a lot of it sits inside companies and never gets published. So you can't just scrape your way to a solution there.

The way I think about it is in layers. At the bottom you have the more fundamental, physical understanding: structures, interactions, how molecules fit together. That's where you can build very general models that transfer. Then you stack more specific, task-oriented learning on top, where you might have far less data but you're starting from a much richer representation. The better that foundation, the less downstream data you need.

And then the other piece is that you don't have to treat data as fixed. One of the exciting things is closing the loop: using models to decide which experiments to run, generating data that's maximally informative rather than just more of the same. So I'd say data is a constraint, absolutely, but it's one you can engineer around through better models, better use of existing data, and being much more deliberate about the data you go out and create.

r001.rationale: The response says data is a constraint but argues better models and existing data enable progress, and describes generating informative experiments to work around scarcity.

r002.rationale: It notes that some data is noisy, generated under different conditions, and unpublished, but does not state that historical biological data was not collected specifically to train machine learning models.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is a question I get asked a lot, and I think the honest answer is that it's the wrong framing, or at least it's a framing that hides the interesting part. People look at what happened in language and vision, where you had this enormous pool of data sitting on the internet, and the breakthrough was in large part figuring out how to actually use it at scale. And then they look at biology and say, well, we don't have the internet of biology, so we're stuck.

I don't think we're stuck. I think the difference is that in biology you can go and generate the data. The internet was a sort of happy accident for language models. In biology we actually get to design the data-generating process, and that's a much more powerful position to be in if you take it seriously. The question becomes less "is there enough data" and more "what data should exist, and how do you build the loop that creates it."

So the way I think about it is as a flywheel. You have models that make predictions about some biological system, say which molecules bind to which proteins, or how a cell responds to a perturbation. Those predictions are wrong in interesting ways. You run experiments that are specifically chosen to resolve where the model is most uncertain, or where being right matters most. That data goes back into the model, the model gets better, and the next round of experiments gets more informative. It's active learning, but at the scale of a lab rather than a dataset.

And that means the real bottleneck isn't data in the abstract. It's the quality and the interface of the experimental platform. Can you run experiments fast enough, reproducibly enough, and in a form where the output is something a model can learn from? A lot of historical biology data is actually quite hard to learn from, not because it's small, but because it was generated by different labs, under different conditions, with different assays, and the noise structure is a mess. Ten thousand clean, consistent measurements that you designed to be informative can be worth more than a million scraped from the literature.

The other thing I'd say is that biology has a lot of inductive structure that lets you be data-efficient in a way that's hard in some other domains. Physics constrains what proteins can do. Evolution has already run an enormous experiment for us, and sequence databases encode a lot of that. So you're not starting from zero. The models can bootstrap off structure that's already there, and then the experimental loop fills in what evolution didn't bother to explore, which is exactly the region you care about when you're trying to design a drug.

So, is data a bottleneck? In the sense that you can't just download your way to a solution, sure. But I'd rather have a problem where I can build the data engine than one where I'm limited to whatever happens to be lying around.

r001.rationale: The response says biology is not stuck for lack of data: data can be generated through designed experiments and an iterative model–experiment loop. It distinguishes data limitations from a barrier that prevents meaningful progress.

r002.rationale: The response says historical data is difficult to learn from because it comes from different labs, conditions, and assays, but does not clearly state that it was not generated specifically to train machine-learning models.

astra-6.text:
I think data is a bottleneck, but it’s not just a question of how much data you have. It’s whether you have the right data for the problem you’re trying to solve. In biology, you can have very large datasets that capture observations, but what you often want to know is: if I intervene in this system, what’s going to happen? And the data you have may not answer that question.

That’s why I’m excited about the relationship between machine learning and experiments. You can use a model to decide which experiment would be most informative, run that experiment, and feed the result back into the model. Then you’re not simply waiting for more data to become available—you’re actively generating the data that helps you make progress.

So I’d think about it as a bottleneck in that whole learning loop: the quality of the measurements, which experiments you can do, and how quickly you can learn from them.

r001.rationale: It describes data as a bottleneck because existing observations may not answer intervention questions, then proposes generating informative data through experiments. It does not distinguish these constraints from a bottleneck that prevents meaningful progress with currently available or presently generatable data.

r002.rationale: The response says existing datasets capture observations, but does not state that historical biological data was not generated specifically to train machine learning models.

sol-6.1.text:
I think data is a bottleneck, but it’s useful to ask what kind of data we’re missing. There’s a huge amount of biological data out there, but that doesn’t necessarily mean you have the right data to answer a particular question or make a particular prediction.

A lot of what we have is observational. You can learn very powerful representations from that, but if you want to understand what happens when you change something—perturb a protein, introduce a mutation, apply a drug—you need data that captures those interventions. And you need measurements that are reliable and relevant to the thing you’re trying to achieve.

So I think the exciting opportunity is to bring machine learning and experimentation into a much tighter loop. The model helps you decide which experiment would be most informative, you run that experiment, and the result improves the model. Then the question becomes less ‘Have we run out of data?’ and more ‘How efficiently can we generate the data that will actually move us forward?’

r001.rationale: The response says data is a bottleneck and points to missing intervention data, but does not distinguish those constraints from a bottleneck that prevents meaningful progress with available or currently generatable data.

r002.rationale: It describes much existing data as observational, but does not say historical biological data was not generated specifically for training machine learning models.
